auth.close: Social Darwinism applied Charles Darwin's theory of "survival of the fittest" to human society and economics. Proponents like Herbert Spencer and William Graham Sumner argued that wealth and success were indicators of natural superiority, while poverty indicated weakness. This philosophy was used to justify laissez-faire capitalism, oppose government regulation, and resist social welfare programs. Business leaders embraced these ideas to defend monopolies, low wages, and opposition to labor reforms. The Social Gospel was a Protestant reform movement that applied Christian ethics to social problems. Leaders like Walter Rauschenbusch argued that Christians had a duty to address poverty, unsafe working conditions, and urban problems. The movement taught that salvation involved not just individual souls but also transforming society to reflect Christian values of justice and compassion. Social Gospel advocates supported settlement houses like Jane Addams' Hull House, labor reforms, and government intervention to improve society. These competing philosophies shaped debates over government's role in addressing inequality. Social Darwinism supported the status quo of industrial capitalism, arguing that helping the poor was futile and even harmful. The Social Gospel provided moral justification for Progressive Era reforms, arguing that Christians must work to create a more just society. The tension between these viewpoints continues to influence debates about welfare, regulation, and the role of government today.

auth.close: Booker T. Washington (1856-1915) was born into slavery in Virginia and rose to found Tuskegee Institute in Alabama. His 1895 Atlanta Compromise speech made him the most prominent African American leader of his era. W.E.B. Du Bois (1868-1963) was born free in Massachusetts and became the first African American to earn a Ph.D. from Harvard. He co-founded the NAACP (1909) and challenged Washington's approach in his book "The Souls of Black Folk" (1903). Their different origins shaped their different philosophies. Washington emphasized vocational and industrial training to prepare African Americans for jobs in agriculture and trades. He believed economic self-sufficiency would gradually lead to respect and equal rights. Du Bois advocated for classical liberal arts education, especially for the "Talented Tenth"—the top 10% of African Americans who would become leaders and professionals to lift up the entire race. Du Bois argued that limiting education to vocational training would permanently consign African Americans to second-class status. Washington favored accommodation and gradualism, publicly accepting segregation temporarily while working behind the scenes for civil rights. He believed economic progress would eventually lead to social and political equality without direct confrontation. Du Bois demanded immediate civil and political rights, opposing accommodation and calling for direct action to secure voting rights, end segregation, and achieve full equality. He founded the Niagara Movement (1905) and later the NAACP to fight through political and legal means. Washington discouraged political agitation, working instead through economic development and relationships with white philanthropists and politicians. He built a powerful network called the "Tuskegee Machine" that influenced patronage and funding. Du Bois advocated for political activism, legal challenges, and organized protest. He believed African Americans should vote, run for office, and use every legal means to achieve equality. These competing strategies represented fundamental disagreements about how oppressed people should seek justice.

auth.close: Populism was a political movement representing farmers and laborers who felt exploited by big business, railroads, and banks. Populists sought government regulation of monopolies, currency reform, and greater democratic participation to protect common people from wealthy elites. The movement emerged from agricultural distress as farmers faced falling crop prices, high railroad shipping rates, and crushing debt. Populism represented the first major challenge to industrial capitalism's dominance of American politics. The Patrons of Husbandry (Grangers), founded in 1867 by Oliver Kelley, organized farmers into cooperatives to bypass middlemen and lobbied for state laws regulating railroad rates and grain elevator charges (Granger Laws). The Farmers' Alliance, more politically active than the Grangers, organized cooperatives, pushed for government ownership of railroads, and formed the foundation of the People's Party (Populist Party) in 1892. These organizations gave farmers political voice and demonstrated the power of collective action. Farmers faced discriminatory pricing from railroads that charged more for short hauls than long hauls and gave rebates to big shippers while gouging small farmers. Railroad monopolies controlled the only means of getting crops to market, leaving farmers no alternatives. Grain elevator operators, often connected to railroads, charged excessive storage fees. These grievances led farmers to demand government regulation of railroads as common carriers serving the public interest, not just private profit. Populists demanded fundamental economic reforms: banking reform through an end to the gold standard and adoption of bimetallism (gold and silver currency) to inflate the money supply, raise crop prices, and ease farmers' debts; a graduated income tax to shift the tax burden from farmers to wealthy industrialists; government ownership or regulation of railroads, telegraph, and telephone as public utilities; direct election of senators; and secret ballot voting. Many of these reforms were later adopted during the Progressive Era.

auth.close: Rapid industrialization created dangerous working conditions with workers facing 10-16 hour workdays, low wages often below subsistence level, and no job security. Child labor was widespread, and economic depressions caused unemployment and wage cuts. Immigration provided cheap labor that undercut American workers' bargaining power. These conditions drove workers to organize unions for collective bargaining, workplace safety, and fair wages. Labor unions employed various tactics to pressure employers: strikes (work stoppages), boycotts (refusing to buy products from anti-union companies), collective bargaining (negotiating as a group), picketing (protesting outside workplaces), and solidarity (supporting other unions during disputes). These tactics gave workers leverage they lacked as individuals, though employers and government often responded with force. Eugene Debs led the American Railway Union and organized the Pullman Strike (1894). Imprisoned for defying federal court injunctions, he later became a Socialist Party presidential candidate, advocating for industrial unions that included all workers regardless of skill. Samuel Gompers founded and led the American Federation of Labor (AFL), focusing on "bread and butter" issues—wages, hours, working conditions—rather than political revolution. He organized skilled workers into craft unions and avoided radical politics, making the AFL the dominant labor organization. Tennessee leased convicts to private companies as cheap labor, undermining free miners' wages. When convicts were used to break a strike at Coal Creek (1891-1892), armed miners freed the prisoners and burned the stockades. The conflict led to military intervention but eventually ended the convict lease system in Tennessee. This episode demonstrated how prison labor was used against free workers and how workers could challenge unjust systems through direct action. Management used strikebreakers ("scabs"), private security forces like the Pinkertons, blacklists of union members, and lockouts to break unions. Labor unions employed various tactics to pressure employers: strikes (work stoppages), boycotts (refusing to buy products from anti-union companies), collective bargaining (negotiating as a group), picketing (protesting outside workplaces), and solidarity (supporting other unions during disputes). auth.close: Progressives sought to increase democratic participation and government accountability, regulate big business and break up monopolies, improve working and living conditions, eliminate political corruption, promote social justice and moral reform, and use scientific methods to solve social problems. The movement drew support from middle-class reformers, journalists, social workers, and some business leaders who believed capitalism needed reform to survive. Progressive reforms expanded direct democracy: Initiative allowed citizens to propose laws through petition. Referendum let voters approve or reject laws passed by legislatures. Recall enabled voters to remove elected officials before their terms ended. These reforms reduced the power of political machines and corrupt officials by giving citizens direct control over legislation and officeholders, making government more responsive to public will. Direct primaries replaced party conventions for selecting candidates. Previously, party bosses chose nominees in smoke-filled rooms, giving voters only the choice between pre-selected candidates. Primaries let ordinary voters participate in choosing nominees, reducing the control of party machines and increasing democratic participation. This reform spread from Wisconsin to most states and remains the standard method for selecting candidates today. The 16th Amendment (1913) gave Congress power to levy income taxes without apportionment among states, enabling progressive taxation and funding expanded government programs. The 17th Amendment (1913) provided for direct election of senators by popular vote instead of state legislatures, reducing corruption and making the Senate more responsive to voters. The 18th Amendment (1919) established Prohibition, banning alcohol manufacture and sale—a reform later repealed by the 21st Amendment (1933) due to unintended consequences.

He positioned the federal government as a neutral mediator between competing interests rather than always siding with business. The Square Deal called for regulation of big business when necessary and conservation of natural resources for future generations. It established the precedent that the federal government had a responsibility to ensure economic fairness and protect the public interest. Motivated by Upton Sinclair's "The Jungle," patent medicine scandals, and consumer safety concerns, Roosevelt pushed for food and drug regulation. The Pure Food and Drug Act (1906) prohibited mislabeled and adulterated food and drugs, requiring ingredient labeling and creating the foundation for the FDA. The Meat Inspection Act (1906) required federal inspection of meat processing facilities and sanitary standards, restoring confidence in American meat products. Roosevelt distinguished between "good trusts" (efficient, fair to consumers) and "bad trusts" (abusive, monopolistic). He used the Sherman Antitrust Act selectively, negotiating with some corporations while prosecuting others. Major cases included breaking up the Northern Securities Company (1904) and later supporting the Standard Oil breakup. This demonstrated that the federal government had power over big business and would use it to restore competition. Roosevelt believed in "conservation means development as much as it does protection." He expanded the national park system with 5 new parks, created 150 national forests covering 148 million acres, established 51 federal bird sanctuaries, and supported the Newlands Act (1902) for western irrigation. Roosevelt established conservation as a federal responsibility, balancing economic development with environmental preservation.

This contrasted with Roosevelt's "New Nationalism," which accepted large corporations but regulated them heavily. Wilson's philosophy was summed up as giving "a man with a dollar in his pocket" a fair chance against concentrated wealth. The Federal Reserve Act addressed problems exposed by the Panic of 1907: financial instability, inflexible currency, and concentrated banking power. The system created 12 regional Federal Reserve Banks overseen by a Federal Reserve Board in Washington. Member banks hold reserves with their regional Fed. The Fed stabilized the banking system and remains central to American economic policy today. The National Park Service was established to manage the growing system of national parks and monuments. The NPS professionalized park management, standardized conservation policies, and balanced public access with preservation. It remains responsible for America's national parks, monuments, and historic sites. Wilson's administration also achieved the Clayton Antitrust Act (1914), which strengthened antitrust laws and protected unions from antitrust prosecution. The Federal Trade Commission (1914) was created to enforce antitrust and consumer protection laws. The Underwood Tariff (1913) reduced tariffs and included the first permanent income tax under the new 16th Amendment. vocab.def: The movement to secure voting rights for women, culminating in the 19th Amendment (1920) after more than 70 years of organized activism.
Ratified on August 18, 1920, this amendment prohibits denying any citizen the right to vote based on sex — extending the vote to women across the United States.
NAWSA president who developed the 'Winning Plan' — a coordinated state-level and federal strategy that led to the 19th Amendment's ratification.
Militant suffragist who founded the National Woman's Party, organized the 1913 Washington parade, led White House picketing, and endured imprisonment and force-feeding for the cause.
Tennessee suffragist who founded the Nashville Equal Suffrage League and built statewide organizing that made Tennessee the decisive 'Perfect 36' for ratification.
The nickname for Tennessee's decisive role as the 36th and final state to ratify the 19th Amendment on August 18, 1920 — secured by Harry T. Burn's deciding vote.

Motivations included belief in natural rights and equality, desire to influence moral and social reforms, response to "taxation without representation," and inspiration from international suffrage movements. The movement took 72 years from Seneca Falls to the 19th Amendment. Carrie Chapman Catt led the National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA) using the "Winning Plan" that coordinated state-by-state and federal campaigns. Anne Dallas Dudley, a Nashville socialite, founded the Nashville Equal Suffrage League and was crucial in securing Tennessee's ratification. Alice Paul founded the National Woman's Party and used more militant tactics including picketing, protests, and hunger strikes. Paul's "Silent Sentinels" picketed the White House, using publicity and confrontation to maintain pressure for a federal amendment. Suffragists employed diverse tactics: traditional methods like lobbying, petitions, speaking tours, and parades; state campaigns to build momentum toward a federal amendment; publicity through dramatic parades, banners, and publications; militant tactics including picketing, civil disobedience, and hunger strikes in prison; and coalition building with other reform movements. Tennessee's August 18, 1920 vote was the crucial 36th state. The legislature was closely divided with intense lobbying from both sides. Young legislator Harry Burn changed his vote after receiving a letter from his mother urging him to "be a good boy" and vote for suffrage. Tennessee's vote enfranchised approximately 26 million women in time for the 1920 presidential election.
close_sections: Historical Context and Motivations

The women's suffrage movement emerged from the abolitionist movement, with the Seneca Falls Convention (1848) marking its formal beginning. Social changes including women's increased education, employment, and reform activities created momentum. Motivations included belief in natural rights and equality, desire to influence moral and social reforms, response to "taxation without representation," and inspiration from international suffrage movements. The movement took 72 years from Seneca Falls to the 19th Amendment.
Key Leaders and Their Strategies

Carrie Chapman Catt led the National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA) using the "Winning Plan" that coordinated state-by-state and federal campaigns. Anne Dallas Dudley, a Nashville socialite, founded the Nashville Equal Suffrage League and was crucial in securing Tennessee's ratification. Alice Paul founded the National Woman's Party and used more militant tactics including picketing, protests, and hunger strikes. Paul's "Silent Sentinels" picketed the White House, using publicity and confrontation to maintain pressure for a federal amendment.
Suffragette Activities and Tactics

Suffragists employed diverse tactics: traditional methods like lobbying, petitions, speaking tours, and parades; state campaigns to build momentum toward a federal amendment; publicity through dramatic parades, banners, and publications; militant tactics including picketing, civil disobedience, and hunger strikes in prison; and coalition building with other reform movements. Women endured arrests, force-feeding during hunger strikes, and violence to advance their cause.
The 19th Amendment and Tennessee as the "Perfect 36"

The 19th Amendment states: "The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged...on account of sex." Ratification required 36 states. Tennessee's August 18, 1920 vote was the crucial 36th state. The legislature was closely divided with intense lobbying from both sides. Young legislator Harry Burn changed his vote after receiving a letter from his mother urging him to "be a good boy" and vote for suffrage. Tennessee's vote enfranchised approximately 26 million women in time for the 1920 presidential election.
